video_title: Steve Hanke Warns: A Financial Crisis Could Send Stocks Down 40%
gist: Johns Hopkins economist Steve Hanke argues AI investment (~5.2% of GDP, accounting for 96% of Q3 growth) is an unprecedented credit-fueled malinvestment with roughly a 40% probability of a financial crisis, implying ~70% downside in AI stocks and ~40% in broad markets followed by a slow, U-shaped recovery. With no fiscal room (6% deficits, $1.7T defense budget, Iran war costs) and inflation forcing the Fed (under Kevin Warsh) to tighten, he expects the bond bear market to continue with the 10-year above 5%, and recommends parking new liquidity in money market funds.

insights.claim: Steve Hanke estimates US AI investment is running at about 5.2% of GDP, far exceeding prior investment booms: canals (1836-41) 0.7%, railroads (1870-90) 2.2%, electrification (1905-25) 0.5%, highways (1950s-60s) 1.1%, and the telecom bubble 1.1%.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: AI capex is roughly 2-5x any historical infrastructure boom as a share of GDP, magnifying both the bubble risk and the macro spillover if spending reverses.
insights.quote: there's just nothing like it. It it it it's absolutely massive

insights.claim: Hanke says 96% of the 3.4% annualized US Q3 GDP growth was accounted for by AI investment, meaning the rest of the US economy is essentially flat.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Headline GDP strength masks a stagnant non-AI economy; any AI capex pullback would hit growth directly and expose underlying weakness.
insights.quote: 96% of that was accounted for by AI which which means the rest of the economy right now is is totally flat

insights.claim: Hanke cites projections showing a 58% revenue shortfall versus what AI investment over the next five years would need to earn even a 10% return on capital, implying the revenue cannot finance the buildout.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A large gap between capex and monetization points to eventual capex cuts or write-downs; watch AI revenue versus capex guidance.
insights.quote: there's a 58% revenue shortfall

insights.claim: Hanke frames the AI boom as Austrian-school malinvestment: most companies that jumped on the bandwagon will lose, a few will win, and the sector's market cap is too high and will come down.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Expect dispersion and broad-based losses within AI; avoid owning the whole basket and favor picking the few durable winners, or stay out.
insights.quote: everybody jumped on this bandwagon and and and there'll be a few on the bandwagon that win, but most of them will not

insights.claim: Hanke highlights Apple as a notable exception that has largely stayed out of the AI investment race despite being one of the great companies and stocks of all time.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Companies penalized for under-investing in AI (e.g., Apple) could be relative winners if the AI capex cycle busts.
insights.quote: Apple looks like it's it's stayed out of the the game

insights.claim: Hanke cites a 2022 Journal of Finance paper by Greenwood and co-authors finding that simultaneous rapid credit expansion and rising sector valuations raise the probability of a financial crisis to about 40%, versus a baseline of about 7%.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Use the credit-plus-valuation dual surge as a bubble-risk screen; AI currently meets both conditions.
insights.quote: That's a pure crisis would increase to about 40% if you had these dual things of overextension of credit and in increases in valuation

insights.claim: Hanke says AI stocks are already down about 25% from their peak, but if the bubble pops they would fall about 70%, with collateral damage of roughly a 40% decline in the general stock market.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Current AI drawdown may be early innings; size equity exposure for a potential 40% broad-market drawdown scenario.
insights.quote: if if it pops it'll go down about 70 %. And the collateral damage in the in the general markets will probably be a reduction of maybe 40 %

insights.claim: Hanke likens the AI setup to the 2007-2008 housing bust, where a huge credit expansion coincided with surging house valuations before the bubble popped.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: The analog implies spillover from a sector bust into the wider financial system, not just a contained tech correction.

insights.claim: Hanke says it is uncertain whether an overvalued bubble pops or deflates slowly, but popping usually happens when the bubble coincides with tightening monetary policy.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Fed tightening is the trigger to watch for a disorderly AI unwind versus a slow deflation.
insights.quote: So everything is always about monetary policy. People forget.

insights.claim: Hanke expects a recession following the AI malinvestment to have a slow, long-slog recovery rather than a V-shaped bounce, because the malinvestment is massive and touches many sectors including electricity and commodities.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Don't bank on a quick buy-the-dip recovery; drawdowns could persist, hurting AI-adjacent energy and commodity plays too.
insights.quote: It's going to be probably a long slog

insights.claim: Hanke says he is not predicting a crisis outright but sees a non-trivial chance of one, calling AI the biggest thing in the economy that investors must watch closely.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Frame as a probabilistic tail risk to hedge, not a certain call.
insights.quote: I'm not predicting that it's going to happen, but but it it it's it's [laughter] again to use my non-trivial there's a non-trivial chance that it will

insights.claim: Hanke says hyperscalers initially funded AI with free cash flow, burned through it, and then moved heavily into the debt market, and their credit default swap spreads are now widening.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Widening hyperscaler CDS shows bond investors are already pricing AI risk; track CDS and debt issuance as early warnings.
insights.quote: So so the the bond vigilante smell some of this stuff out pretty quickly

insights.claim: Hanke says the first-order losses from an AI bust would fall on private credit and non-bank lenders, but would likely come back to haunt banks because banks have extended credit to those non-banks.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Bank exposure to non-bank lenders is the contagion channel; watch bank lending to private credit vehicles.
insights.quote: it often comes back to haunt the the banks because the the the the banks have extended credit to these other non-banks

insights.claim: Hanke says the AI boom will stop when the credit spigot is turned off, i.e., when the money runs out.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Monitor credit availability for AI buildouts (bond spreads, private credit flows) as the key tell for the boom's end.

insights.claim: Hanke says that if the AI bubble pops into a true financial crisis entangling banks, the Fed would be forced to pump liquidity into markets despite its inflation problem.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A crisis scenario likely flips the Fed from tightening to liquidity injection, a key regime shift for rates and risk assets.
insights.quote: the Fed always reacts pretty rapidly to a financial crisis

insights.claim: Hanke expects the Democratic midterm win to change little for the economy because neither party is interested in controlling spending, deficits, or debt; interest costs will take a growing share of federal spending.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Don't expect fiscal consolidation from divided government; persistent deficits support higher term premia.
insights.quote: it's a bipartisan deal

insights.claim: Hanke says with a deficit of about 6% of GDP for a long time, there is no fiscal firepower to stimulate out of an AI-bust recession, and the Fed cannot loosen without risking stagflation.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Policy backstops are weaker than in past downturns, raising downside severity and duration.
insights.quote: There is no margin of safety.

insights.claim: Hanke attributes the post-pandemic inflation to M2 money supply growth of about 27% per year, the highest since the Fed's founding in 1913, rather than supply-chain disruptions.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Under a monetarist lens, money supply growth is the key inflation indicator to track.

insights.claim: Hanke estimates reducing federal debt to even 90% of GDP would realistically take five to 10 years of budget control.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Fiscal repair is a multi-year process; no near-term relief for bond supply pressure.

insights.claim: Citing David Stockman's analysis, Hanke says genuinely defending the US costs about $850 billion a year, while the defense budget is heading to $1.7 trillion, roughly double.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Defense spending is a major, sticky driver of deficits and Treasury supply; supportive for defense contractors, negative for bonds.

insights.claim: Hanke estimates the Iran war, with acknowledged spending approaching $50 billion, will ultimately cost about $1 trillion in direct costs including restocking munitions.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: War costs add further deficit pressure and munitions restocking demand.
insights.quote: I have estimated that the end of the day this thing will cost a trillion dollars

insights.claim: Hanke says the bond bear market that began in 2022 will continue, following a 39-year bond bull market that started in 1981, noting bond markets have very long bull and bear cycles.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Avoid long-duration Treasuries; secular rate trend is up.
insights.quote: the bear market that we've been in bonds since 2022 will will continue

insights.claim: Hanke expects the 10-year US Treasury yield to stay above 5% for quite some time.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Elevated benchmark yields keep mortgage and private borrowing costs high, pressuring housing and equity valuations.
insights.quote: I think it will stay up over 5% for quite some time.

insights.claim: Hanke says interest-rate-based models imply the Fed funds rate would need to rise by 2.5 to 3 percentage points from current levels to be consistent with a 2% inflation target, so short-end rates will likely keep rising.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Markets pricing cuts may be wrong; short-end rate risk is to the upside absent a crisis.

insights.claim: Hanke views new Fed chair Kevin Warsh positively for focusing on hitting 2% inflation and paying attention to money supply; Divisia M4 is growing about 7.4% year over year and getting it to 5-6% would deliver 2% inflation.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Watch broad money growth (Divisia M4) falling toward 5-6% as the signal that inflation will return to target.

insights.claim: Hanke says the public dislikes AI and the Silicon Valley crowd, opposes data centers locally, and a newly elected Democratic governor (e.g., in Texas) could move to shut data center construction down.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Political and permitting risk to data center buildouts is rising after the midterms.
insights.quote: the public does not like AI

insights.claim: Hanke describes data centers as a boomtown effect: local construction jobs for a year or so, then capital-intensive sites that employ few people and leave pollution behind.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Explains durable local opposition to data centers, a headwind to AI infrastructure siting.
insights.quote: These things are capital intensive. They're not labor intensive.

insights.claim: Hanke says net wealth of Americans under 35 deteriorated sharply from 2022 through 2025, which explains young voters turning against Trump and the Republicans more than specific cost-of-living items.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Youth balance-sheet stress may drive redistributive tax and affordability policy going forward.
insights.quote: there's nothing more important than a balance sheet

insights.claim: Hanke argues the West has entered an 'age of big players' (since the COVID lockdowns) colliding with an 'age of resentment' against Trump, Silicon Valley, the crypto crowd and Washington, with leaders in the UK, France and Germany lacking legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Populist backlash raises regulatory and political risk for tech, crypto and elite-associated sectors.
insights.quote: the deadly cocktail is a mixture of the age of big players versus the age of resentment

insights.claim: Hanke criticizes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent as floundering, unpopular and a hawk on Iran sanctions alongside Hegseth, saying he is unlikely to deliver a credible dramatic reset such as a gold revaluation or stablecoin scheme.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Don't count on a Treasury policy rabbit-out-of-the-hat to defuse debt pressures.
insights.quote: sanctions are a weapon of war just like a a missile or a or a destroyer

insights.claim: Hanke recommends putting any additional liquidity into money market funds rather than the stock market, given his clear view that AI is coming down and a broadly foggy outlook.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Defensive cash positioning; new capital to money markets until the AI unwind plays out.
insights.quote: I wouldn't be putting them in the stock market. I'd be putting them in a money market fund.
